channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Judge denies request by Elon Musk’s xAI to pause Minnesota nudification ban
item.description: NBC News: “A federal judge on Friday denied a request from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI to block a Minnesota law that will be the first in the nation to ban nudification technology.”

item.title: Most teens still on social media three months after under-16 ban began, study finds
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “More than eight in 10 Australian teenagers under 16 are still using social media three months on from the national ban. Despite a decrease in account ownership, children aged 10 to 15 are using social media just as frequently as before the ban.”

item.title: Open source project fools AI scrapers with poisoned font
item.description: The Register: “Look at a web page written using a ShieldFont font and it’ll appear exactly as one would expect: All the content words (the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs that give a sentence meaning) are the same as the writer originally wrote. Inspect the raw HTML that a scraper reads from a ShieldFonted page, however, and you’ll see a sentence that’s essentially gibberish.”

item.title: For Museum Boss Who Became a Trump Target, It’s Déjà Vu All Over Again
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Kim Sajet left as director of the National Portrait Gallery when she found herself in the White House cross hairs. Now she’s watching another Smithsonian chief go through it.”

item.title: YouTube Bans Popular ASMR Artists, Accusing Them of Making ‘Sexually Gratifying’ Content
item.description: 404 Media: “So far, YouTube creators affected by the wave of bans who’ve spoken publicly about YouTube removing their channels include ItsBunniiASMR, Slight Sounds, Nananightray, Roseasmr, Simoneasmr, and Janina Wilhelmsen, all of whom had significant followings on the platform. There are still many ASMR creators on YouTube, making the bans even more confusing.”

item.title: French student pleads guilty and is fined for a straw-licking stunt in Singapore
item.description: Associated Press: “A French student was fined 600 Singapore dollars ($465) after pleading guilty Thursday to a public nuisance charge in Singapore for filming himself licking a straw from an orange juice vending machine and putting it back in what lawyers described as a social media stunt.”

item.title: Announcing the DRP Metadata Analyst
item.description: Data Rescue Project: “Today’s post is an interview with our new Metadata Analyst! The DRP is grateful to be able to offer this position throught the generous support of the Portfolio to Protect Science, a fiscally sponsored initiative of Global Impact, as well as other anonymous individual donors.”

item.title: This 3D Blockbuster recreation brings back the video store browsing that streaming killed
item.description: How-To Geek: “Walking through the aisles of a video store used to be half the fun of a movie night. You judged films by their cover art, stumbled across forgotten classics, and often left with something you never planned to watch. A new site called Bingebuster brings back that experience with a fully explorable 3D recreation of a Blockbuster Video store that you can visit right from your browser.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: A designer just put 1,300+ restored 19th-century wildlife illustrations online for free
item.description: Notebook Check: “Nicholas Rougeux is a well-known designer whose previous restoration projects include Euclid’s Elements, Pierre-Joseph Redouté’s Les Roses and Les Liliacées, and Elizabeth Twining’s Illustrations of the Natural Orders of Plants. He has now put a complete digital reproduction of The Naturalist’s Library online — it’s a Victorian-era series of 40 volumes covering everything from birds and bees to quadrupeds and marsupials.”

item.title: Google Related Searches Based On Your Browsing
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google is now testing showing related searches based on your browsing. I suspect this is based on your browsing history on Chrome, beyond what you may search for in Google but based on what pages you browse.”

item.title: Trump aide who bet on the president’s speeches no longer works for the government
item.description: Politico: “Gabriel Perez, the White House staffer who allegedly used his advanced knowledge of President Donald Trump’s speeches to place bets on the prediction market Kalshi, no longer works for the federal government, a White House official said Tuesday. The official, granted anonymity to discuss the matter, declined to answer questions about whether Perez was fired.”

item.title: How absurdist memes turned into war propaganda
item.description: Financial Times: “If Russia’s invasion of Ukraine was the first TikTok war, then the Iran conflict is the first meme war. While Trump is on Truth Social, official Iranian accounts have embarked on their own trolling campaign via X. The Iranian embassy in Zimbabwe joked that it had lost the keys to the Strait of Hormuz and posted a creepy AI image of a zombified Jeffrey Epstein smiling at the destruction of Iranian hospitals. The Iranian embassy in South Africa posted a strange, AI-generated video of Trump singing about blockades.”

item.title: People Are Generating a Flood of Fake News About Trump That Does No Reputational Damage Whatsoever
item.description: Gizmodo: “President Donald Trump regularly posts some of the most bizarre content on the internet, from images of himself as Jesus Christ to AI videos of diarrhea being dumped on liberal protesters. But there’s been a weird trend over the past year: social media users take Trump’s strange fake photos and make them only slightly weirder. And then those fakes go viral, with most people never realizing they’re looking at something Trump never actually posted.”

item.title: MHC launches new Mississippi Stories Grant program
item.description: Jackson Advocate: “The Mississippi Humanities Council (MHC) has launched the Mississippi Stories Grant, a new funding opportunity to help communities across the state preserve, share, and celebrate the voices and lived experiences of Mississippians. The program is supported by the Mississippi Legislature through the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH).”

item.title: Tucson man files claim alleging deputies ignored swatting warnings before shooting left him paralyzed
item.description: KGUN: “A Tucson man who was left paralyzed after being shot by Pima County sheriff’s deputies during a response to what his attorneys say was a false ‘swatting’ call has filed a Notice of Claim against Pima County, Sheriff Chris Nanos and numerous sheriff’s employees, alleging deputies ignored clear warning signs that the emergency was a hoax. The claim was filed on behalf of 24-year-old Axeel Melendez and his mother, Carmen Melendez, over the April 10, 2026, shooting at their home.”

item.title: AFL clubs explore facial recognition as new ticketing method
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “Facial recognition technology (FRT) is being rolled out in Australia as an alternative to digital or paper tickets for live events. The Geelong Football Club has made it available to its members, while technology provider Wicket says it is in ‘active discussions’ with other AFL clubs.”

item.title: 5th Circuit blocks Texas law requiring websites to filter “harmful” speech
item.description: Ars Technica: “Texas cannot enforce a law’s requirement that websites block minors from seeing harmful speech, the US Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit ruled on Friday.”

item.title: Betting on Drug Trials and Approvals Prompts Concerns About Undermining Research
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “On the betting websites Kalshi and Polymarket, people can now wager on whether the Food and Drug Administration will decide this year to approve medicines for cancers of the lung, breast, pancreas and blood. Kalshi also plans to allow users to bet on whether drug trials will succeed. Researchers, doctors and patients said that these prediction markets threaten to undermine the drug development process.”

item.title: LTE Data Rescue Success: 25 Years of Data Digitized
item.description: ZALF: “Almost 90 years of long-term experiments (LTEs) at the Research Station of Thyrow of the Humboldt University of Berlin (HU) serve as the foundation for a valuable dataset in the BonaRes Repository.”

item.title: You can now play Morrowind directly in your browser, no installation required
item.description: TechSpot: “A browser tab can now run Morrowind’s engine, a game that once pushed desktop hardware to its limits. A new project called OpenMW-Web brings The Elder Scrolls III into a web browser using the OpenMW engine, rather than through streaming or emulation.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Mayor Mamdani Launches LIFT Tracker to Build Affordable Housing on City-owned Land
item.description: New York City: “The tracker maps more than 100 City-owned sites across the five boroughs that will deliver more than 50,000 new homes, making it easier for New Yorkers to follow the City’s progress in bringing new housing online. LIFT also highlights opportunities to pair new housing with public amenities, including libraries and other neighborhood services.”

item.title: Goldfields diary of young Englishman uncovered after 115 years
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “A six-month joint effort between historical societies from opposite sides of the world has recently solved the mystery of a century-old diary. The diary of Gordon Howard Tilly tells the story of a young engineer’s time in Kalgoorlie-Boulder in intricate detail. Its transcript is now available at the Eastern Goldfields Historical Society.”

item.title: Meta‑backed research finds exposure to ‘untrustworthy’ social media is rare. The fine print is less reassuring
item.description: The Conversation: “A new study published today in Science Advances offers the most rigorous answers yet. It comes from a collaboration between Meta and academic researchers who studied the 2020 United States election. It was run from inside the machine – on the live feeds of Facebook and Instagram. The answers sound reassuring: exposure to lies was rare for most users, and removing them did not measurably shift anyone’s beliefs. But, as a researcher who studies how misinformation permeates these platforms, I think the fine print matters more than the headline.”

item.title: Share your World Cup story with UTA Libraries
item.description: UT Arlington: “Following Arlington’s hosting of nine World Cup matches, The University of Texas at Arlington Libraries is inviting soccer fans, residents and visitors from around the globe to help preserve this historic moment by contributing their personal experiences to a new World Cup digital collection.”

item.title: Snap will show off its AR Specs at a September 16 event
item.description: Engadget: “Snap is about to start selling its standalone augmented reality glasses to the public, so of course it’s holding an event to explain what Specs are all about. It takes place in Los Angeles at 7PM ET on September 16. You’ll be able to watch a livestream if you wish.”

item.title: Central Park lawyers’ viral kiss sparks privacy debate
item.description: Mashable: “On July 23, TikTok creator Jay Guapõ, who boasts 3.5 million followers, posted a video showing a man and woman kissing near Central Park West and West 63rd Street. Guapõ approaches them while continuing to record. ‘Get a room. There’s kids around,’ he tells them.”

item.title: A Time Capsule was buried in 1976. Now Nobody Can Find It.
item.description: Syracuse.com: “Nearly 50 years after volunteers buried a time capsule on the Ohio Expo Center grounds during the nation’s 1976 Bicentennial celebration, organizers acknowledge they have been unable to locate the capsule ahead of the 2026 opening that had long been anticipated.”

item.title: With help from data, art museums are reframing the visitor experience
item.description: Ars Technica: “Museums take this educational role seriously, and many institutions understand the need to sustain and broaden their appeal…. To aid this transition, museums and other cultural institutions are increasingly using data to inform decisions about how to present the works they house.”

item.title: Herd of life-size buffalo puppets will make symbolic journey through Brooklyn this fall
item.description: Brooklyn Paper: “On Sept. 19 and 20, a herd of 50 life-size buffalo puppets will roam the streets of Downtown Brooklyn and Manhattan, running amongst New Yorkers and tourists as they visit historic sites and public parks and plazas. Along the way, the herd — operated by a team of 150 volunteer puppeteers — will be joined by actors, civic leaders and marching bands for live music and dance performances and Native American tribal ceremonies.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Wondering about tomorrow’s air quality? Check WSU’s new interactive tool
item.description: Washington State University: “The tool provides information on fine particulate matter and ozone concentrations, as well as fire locations and intensity, smoke layers, meteorological conditions, and other data on an hourly basis for Washington, Oregon and Idaho, along with parts of surrounding states. Enter your location, and it produces a three-day rolling forecast, down to a 4-kilometer grid square.”

item.title: Google launches Street View in Kosovo
item.description: Virtual Streets: “After two years of filming and some intrigue following its absence in the gigantic drop that brought a slew of images in neighboring areas such as Albania, Montenegro, and North Macedonia, it emerged this month.”

item.title: Reddit shares sink 7% on ‘choppy’ search referrals even as results blow past estimates
item.description: CNBC: “Reddit reported second-quarter earnings on Thursday that beat on the top and the bottom lines, and the company issued guidance that sailed past expectations. But the company’s shares sank after it revealed in an investor letter that ‘Search referrals were choppy,’ underscoring investor concerns about Reddit’s reliance on Google to land new users.”

item.title: Army reveals project to digitize Egypt’s radio and television heritage
item.description: Egypt Independent: “In a meeting in el-Alamein, Sisi followed up on the implementation status of the project to archive and digitize Egypt’s radio and television heritage housed in the historic Maspero building, in cooperation with major international companies and relevant state entities.”

item.title: Whaling Museum goes viral for ‘worst aquarium ever’ T-shirts, totes
item.description: New Bedford Light: “New Bedford is considered the home of whaling’s history in America — and now, home to the worst aquarium ever. In 2020, a Google user left a one-star review of the New Bedford Whaling Museum coining that phrase. Last fall, the museum began selling shirts and hoodies with the review on the back and a whale skeleton on the front. Now, the design is capturing national attention.”

item.title: US College Has ‘Content Creation’ Major for Aspiring Social Media Influencers
item.description: PetaPixel: “Arizona State University is now offering a bachelor’s degree in content creation for aspiring social media influencers. The university has launched a new Bachelor of Arts in Content Creation through its Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication, allowing students to earn a four-year degree focused on careers as professional content creators, digital storytellers, and influencers.”

item.title: Indonesia scraps song and music copyright registration fee to build a national music database
item.description: Music Business Worldwide: “Indonesia will stop charging songwriters, performers, and record producers to log their work on the national copyright register. From August 1, 2026, the fee to record a song or musical composition drops from 200,000 rupiah (approx. USD $11) to Rp0.”

item.title: The Pokémon Company is turning to facial recognition scans to help combat scalpers
item.description: PC Gamer: “Nintendo has announced the rollout of a facial recognition system and new entry and purchase rules for its Pokémon stores in Japan. It’s not exactly a last-ditch effort, but it’s yet another attempt at combating scalpers which have been plaguing the hobby ever since its inception.”

item.title: Great Barrier Reef Microbiome Map Reveals 500 New Bacterial Species Hidden In Coral Reef Waters
item.description: Science Times: “A new microbiome map of the Great Barrier Reef has identified more than 500 previously unknown bacterial species and more than 300,000 distinct viruses in open reef waters, according to research published in Nature on July 22, 2026.”

item.title: A fake ‘jelly diet’ has fooled at least one celebrity. You could be next
item.description: The Conversation: “Paris Hilton’s mother Kathy recently tried the ‘Jell-O diet’ to lose weight. She believed other celebrities – Oprah Winfrey, Doctor Oz, Michelle Obama and Kelly Clarkson – had endorsed it. But the diet was fake and so were the endorsements. Both had been generated by artificial intelligence (AI).”

item.title: Will We Ever Solve the Problem of Losing Data?
item.description: Gizmodo: “…for this Giz Asks, we asked experts in computer science, cybersecurity, and archival research to consider the idea of ‘permanence,’ specifically in the context of how we record, track, and store information. That is, is there such a thing as permanent data storage?”

item.title: Team Repair Breaks Things To Teach People How To Fix Them
item.description: Hackaday: “Many people would rather repair what they have than have to get a new device and deal with all the annoyances of shopping and getting used to a new item. The problem is, most people don’t have any experience fixing their broken electronics and are intimidated by the process. [Team Repair] has found that helping people through the process the first time is a big confidence boost, especially when they have a test piece to work with.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: US government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conference
item.description: The Guardian: “A US government map of Africa mislabeled every country during a state department presentation at a ⁠global conference in Brazil ⁠this week, ​causing a stir among attenders who took screenshots and posted them online.”

item.title: In partisan times, are data centers the one thing to unite people
item.description: Georgia Recorder: “We live in intensely partisan times. Depending on the poll and the year, there are either slightly more or less either self-avowed Democrats or Republicans in the nation. The partisanship manifests itself in everything from support or opposition for the war in Iran to the opinions in the way local elections should be run. Enter data centers. In communities where concern over data center development starts to boil, people increasingly are finding ways to look past the usual political labels.”

item.title: How Meta Got Everything It Wanted in a Secret Louisiana Data Center Deal
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Rewriting the bill was a critical part of a nine-month process that Meta used to cut deals behind the scenes, avoid local opposition and offload financial risk, according to interviews with more than 40 people and a review of corporate filings, tax records, property records and meeting transcripts. The secrecy was agreed to by nearly everyone involved, from utility executives to the governor’s office to a local elected official who knew about the talks with Meta and sold 300 acres of his own property for the project.”

item.title: New York school pauses plan to deploy humanlike AI robot teacher after backlash
item.description: Associated Press: “A school district in a rural corner of upstate New York is hitting pause on plans to deploy an AI-powered, humanoid robot in the classroom after state education officials, teachers and local residents raised concerns, including the maker’s ties to a company that produces hyper realistic sex bots.”

item.title: AI Schools, Ballot Initiatives, and Serial Evictors
item.description: Oklahoma Watch: “Maya Henry dives into Alpha School, an expensive, controversial private school system coming to Oklahoma this fall that relies on AI with zero teachers.” This is part of an audio podcast which unfortunately does not look like it has a transcript available.

item.title: AI investor Leopold Aschenbrenner forced to unwind all public stock positions after steep losses, sources say
item.description: CNBC: “The battered $24 billion hedge fund founded by former OpenAI researcher Leopold Aschenbrenner is unwinding many of its trades after big losses on artificial intelligence stocks and a bad bet against software stocks left it scrambling to raise cash, according to people familiar with the matter. The prime brokers for the fund, Situational Awareness, have been rushing to raise cash to meet margin requirements, the people said.”

item.title: The Pentagon wants to build data centers. Congress would like a word.
item.description: Politico: “The Department of Defense’s leasing of land to private companies for artificial intelligence server farms is drawing bipartisan scrutiny from lawmakers worried about the impact on military installations and surrounding communities.”

item.title: VA signs $1.6B contract to integrate AI into agency functions
item.description: Stars and Stripes: “The Department of Veterans Affairs awarded a contract valued up to $1.6 billion to Salesforce — a global cloud-based software company — to develop and integrate artificial intelligence into existing workflows that support customer communication, patient care coordination and the claims approval process, Salesforce announced Friday.”

item.title: Alabama updates ethics guidance for lawyers amid worries about AI misuse
item.description: Reuters: “The Alabama State Bar said lawyers using artificial intelligence cannot charge clients for hours saved by the technology but can bill for time they spend reviewing and ​exercising their judgment over AI-generated work, according to new guidance issued this week.”

item.title: In China, people are renting out their faces to AI
item.description: Rest of World: “The artificial intelligence boom has created a new marketplace in China where people can rent out their faces. A growing number of online platforms are paying people anywhere between $15 and $700 to license their likeness for AI-generated content.”

item.title: Artist sues AI meme generator for selling deeply personal comic as ad template
item.description: Ars Technica: “Artist Elmer Saflor, who goes by the online handle “Superelmer,” loves that millions of people have shared his “Running Away Balloon” comic since it became a popular meme in 2017. However, just because lots of people have copied it, that doesn’t mean it’s OK for an AI meme generator to commercialize his copyrighted meme as a template for who knows how many ads, he told Ars.”

item.title: Google shuts down its Nobel-prize winning AlphaFold project as it focuses on Gemini
item.description: Engadget: “The award-winning team behind Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold program is no more, according to Financial Times. Google has reassigned most of the team’s key members and the original authors of its papers, while a few others have already left the company. AlphaFold is an AI program that can accurately predict three-dimensional structures of proteins from their amino acid sequences in minutes instead of years.”

item.title: In the era of AI slop, human curation is even more important
item.description: Juha-Matti Santala: “Now, more than ever, we need human curation to find anything meaningful. The problem with LLM generated slop is that it requires close to no effort to fill every avenue with it. If you push millions of pieces of content to Youtube, music platforms, app stores and social media every day, it just drowns everything under it due to the sheer volume.” Amen! Support your local human content aggregator! Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: 6.5 million Americans face landslide risks — a new database shows where they live
item.description: University of Washington: “The new Landslide Exposure Database is the first resource to map building-level landslide risk for the entire U.S. The database, developed by University of Washington researchers, rates 128 million buildings by landslide susceptibility, and uses socioeconomic data to assess residents’ vulnerability to the dangers and disruptions caused by landslides.”

item.title: Great Job, Internet!: Comedy Fee Tracker reveals the price of an hour of stand-up
item.description: AV Club: “Using public information obtained through Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests, the Comedy Fee Tracker is a searchable database of talent contracts and payment records from publicly funded venues, such as public colleges and universities, and city, county, and state-owned theaters and arenas.”

item.title: Bing Ads Revenue Up 10%
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Microsoft reported its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings, showing that its search and advertising revenue was up 10%, indicating its ad growth was 2 points lower than the previous quarter. The previous quarter it was up 12%, before that up 10% before that, up 16% and the one before that was 21% and this quarter, it is only up 10%.”

item.title: Yandex reports 16% increase in Q2 revenue, recommends H1 dividend at 110 rbls/share
item.description: Reuters: “Russia’s largest internet-company, Yandex , posts ​a 16% increase in ‌revenue to 386 billion roubles ($4.89 billion) for the ​second quarter of 2026.”

item.title: Telegram literally gives Russia the middle finger after founder Pavel Durov is charged with aiding terrorism
item.description: TechSpot: “Russia has charged Telegram founder and CEO Pavel Durov with ‘aiding terrorism’ and placed him on an international wanted list. The Federal Security Service (FSB) claims the platform failed to remove channels, chats, and bots used by Ukrainian intelligence to organize attacks inside Russia. Telegram’s response was less than diplomatic: its official X account posted a photo of Durov giving the middle finger.”

item.title: I replaced my paid streaming apps with free ones – here’s what surprised me
item.description: ZDNet: “As comfortable as I am with my subscriptions, I never stop looking for ways to save money. So, I figured I’d try some free video and music streaming apps to see if any could replace my big four services. Here’s how it went.”

item.title: From palava huts to TikTok: How Liberians are preserving their past
item.description: Al Jazeera: “Young Liberians are documenting their history, exploring their culture and reaching audiences at home and across the diaspora. Rather than replacing traditional storytellers, they are carrying an age-old tradition into the digital age.”

item.title: Does misinformation on Facebook and Instagram change what you believe?
item.description: UC Berkeley: “The experiment was successful in changing what people saw: participants assigned to the intervention were exposed to roughly 70% less content from untrustworthy sources. However, their political beliefs and attitudes did not measurably change, even among those who were previously exposed to the most content from those sources.”

item.title: This SimCity-Like Visualization Turns Tech’s Most Boring Systems Into Fun
item.description: Gizmodo: “Look, no one has ever accused SQL of being fun. It’s ubiquitous, it’s important, and it’s probably something you need to understand if you’re going to be doing any sort of work with data analytics, web development, and any other field that involves, y’know, data. But fun? Not so much. But maybe that’s just because no-one has ever turned SQL into SimCity.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: ISD Launches the Authoritarian Interference Tracker
item.description: Institute for Strategic Dialogue: “ISD is launching the Authoritarian Interference Tracker (AIT), a tool that catalogues interference operations by Russia, China and Iran across five incident types: cyber operations, kinetic operations, information operations, malign finance, and political and civic subversion.”

item.title: Samsung’s SmartThings API Terminates Free Access
item.description: Hackaday: “If there’s one constant in the world of commercial home automation solutions, it is that of decreasing availability and higher costs as time goes on. So too with Samsung’s SmartThings, the API of which will cease free access in October of 2026. While this does not affect people who use the SmartThings app, any system that relies on access to this API will soon face a $4.99 per month fee for non-commercial users, with various commercial tiers also in the pipeline.”

item.title: Russian Propaganda Is Getting Worse as the War Drags On
item.description: Moscow Times: “In the first months of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia took pride in the high quality of its propaganda. Even its enemies and various analysts were forced to acknowledge that this was one of the few high-quality products the country produced. Four years later, something has broken. It is as if shifting the economy onto a war footing has turned the once-mighty propaganda machine into a rotting pumpkin.”

item.title: Glasgow Life and Creative Scotland join forces on arts centre archive
item.description: The Herald (Scotland): “Last-ditch talks are underway to secure the future of a vast cultural collection spanning half a century which charts the history of two of Glasgow’s best-known arts institutions. The Scottish Government’s arts agency is in talks with Glasgow Life, which runs museums, galleries and cultural venues on behalf of the city council, about acquiring the archive devoted to the Third Eye Centre and the Centre for Contemporary Arts.”

item.title: After hosting another hit concert, Roblox gets more music rights for creators
item.description: Tubefilter: “Roblox wants to be more than just a game-building platform. It wants to become the place you go to hear hit music, and it is amassing the rights deals it needs to make that push. Through a partnership with the indie distribution company Too Lost, Roblox will add a library of tracks from popular artists. Game builders will be able to spruce up their worlds with a soundtrack that includes notable names like Teddy Swims, Alex Warren, and A$ap Ferg.”

item.title: Senior Trump Official Using Government Account To Smear Sitting Federal Judges
item.description: HuffPost: “James Percival, general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, posted a series of messages on social media last week dubbed ‘Worst of the Worst, District Judge Edition.’ … Percival names four U.S. district judges, identifies the Democratic presidents who appointed them and condemns their decisions on immigration-related cases as if they’ve gone beyond the bounds of the law.”

item.title: US FTC sues Hims & Hers for sending user health info to Meta, Snap
item.description: Reuters: “The U.S. Federal Trade ​Commission sued Hims & Hers on Wednesday alleging the telehealth platform shared users’ health ‌data with online advertisers, despite promising privacy, and engaged in deceptive billing and cancellation practices.”

item.title: Why Are Gay Bars Building Databases of Their Patrons?
item.description: Electronic Frontier Foundation: “Recent reports have raised alarm about the use of PatronScan, an ID-checking and face-scanning system, at multiple LGBTQ+ bars in San Francisco’s Castro neighborhood. Much of the attention has focused on reports that the system photographs patrons as they enter venues and questions about whether those images are used for facial recognition. A broader privacy concern also deserves scrutiny.”

item.title: SETI Scientists Think Alien Signals Could Be Hiding in Old Telescope Data
item.description: Gizmodo: “The beauty of Mason and her colleagues’ approach is that it offers a new way to reexamine reams of old data that might already have messages from an alien civilization just waiting for us to hear. From ALMA’s archival data, the team surveyed so-called Band 3 information, with a focus on two high-frequency, narrow-band windows around 90.642 and 93.151 GHz, which have wavelengths in the millimeter and submillimeter range.”

item.title: National Library steps up fight against book-eating pests
item.description: Luxembourg Times: “When people say that someone is devouring literature, they usually mean it in a figurative sense. Unless, that is, we’re talking about a Ctenolepisma longicaudatum, also known as a paper silverfish. You could look up exactly what that is in one of the many encyclopaedias at the Luxembourg National Library (BNL) – provided the silverfish hasn’t been quicker off the mark and already devoured that very information.”

item.title: Thousands of America’s historic landmarks face significant wildfire risk
item.description: UC Santa Barbara: “Researchers at UC Santa Barbara’s National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS) have completed the first national-scale assessment of wildfire risk to American cultural heritage. Of the 100,117 sites listed on the National Register of Historic Places, more than half face measurable wildfire exposure. For 3,446 places, that risk is severe.”

item.title: How camera-equipped homing pigeons could improve robotic vision in flight
item.description: University of British Columbia: “The system weighs just 27 grams and includes a miniature computer, about half the size of a credit card; a tiny modified commercial camera, a motion and orientation measurement unit and cables and electronics tape to reduce static during flight.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Bhoral: The Digital Archive Ensuring Assamese Cinema Is Never Forgotten
item.description: The Story Mug: “In every Assamese household —especially in rural households —the bhoral (granary) remains a symbol of preservation—a place where the harvest is carefully stored for the future. Drawing inspiration from that enduring institution, two passionate admirers of Assamese cinema embarked on a journey to preserve its rich past and evolving present for future generations. The result is Bhoral- which, instead of grains, preserves films, filmmakers and the stories behind them, creating a digital archive for a cinematic legacy that has too often remained scattered, incomplete and at risk of being forgotten.”

item.title: UH digital exhibit connects Asia-Pacific through shared cultural stories
item.description: University of Hawaii: “An ancient glass shard. A mural painted thousands of miles from home. A ceremonial headband passed through generations. These objects tell stories that stretch across generations and oceans in The Ocean That Remembers, a new digital exhibition created through the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s Center for Southeast Asian Studies (CSEAS) and its Asia-Pacific Museum Exchange (APME) program.”

item.title: Elon Musk settles long-running legal battle with X advertisers
item.description: Financial Times: “Elon Musk’s X has settled a long-running legal battle with a group of advertisers, ending a case that accused brands including Mars, Shell, Nestlé and Lego of illegally boycotting the social media platform. X Corp, the parent company of X, took advertisers and the World Federation of Advertisers, a trade body, to court in 2024 claiming that they had conspired to move ‘billions of dollars’ in advertising revenue away from the site.”

item.title: Googling ‘Jimothy’ brings up an unexpected surprise
item.description: Mashable: “On Tuesday, Threads users noticed that Jimothy’s fame has now been acknowledged by the search engine gods — namely, he has his own Google animation.”

item.title: ‘Maxxing’ isn’t the best approach to any part of your health
item.description: CNN: “‘Maxxing’ is an online trend applied to advice for aspects of health including sleep, diet and fertility. But much of this maxxing advice can be unhelpful or unhealthy or go against the steady, personalized changes many experts recommend.”

item.title: Russia accuses Telegram CEO Pavel Durov of aiding terrorism in its latest digital crackdown
item.description: Associated Press: “Russian authorities said Wednesday they had charged Pavel Durov, the founder and CEO of the popular messaging app Telegram, with aiding terrorism, the latest step by the Kremlin to bring the internet and digital communications under its control.”

item.title: New York finalizes social media restrictions for kids
item.description: Spectrum Local News: “[Kathy] Hochul was joined at an announcement by state Attorney General Letitia James, whose office crafted detailed regulations. The rules will apply to the largest social media platforms, including Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat, X and YouTube. Kids under 18 years old will no longer see an addictive algorithmic feed and will no longer receive notifications from midnight to 6 a.m., unless they get parental consent.”

item.title: Connecticut Institutions Win $750,000 National Grant to Preserve the State’s Revolutionary War Records
item.description: Connecticut State Library: “Led by the State Library, a team of Connecticut institutions will conserve, organize, and digitize thousands of pages and objects from Connecticut’s history, then make them freely available online through the Connecticut Digital Archive (CTDA), the Digital Public Library of America (DPLA), and Connecticut Archives Online (CAO).”

item.title: Global climate data, local solutions: 17 new projects from C3S National Collaboration Program kick off
item.description: Copernicus Climate Change Service: “The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) is launching 17 new projects under its National Collaboration Programme (NCP), converting C3S climate data into practical tools for users across Europe and beyond. The initiatives range from operational seasonal and sector-specific forecasting tools to educational resources, and climate adaptation applications tailored to national and regional needs.”

item.title: Rat Shack in Federal Hill leaves droppings people love
item.description: Baltimore Fishbowl: “[Meg] Murray is the creator of Rat Shack, a public art installation she built out of a medicine cabinet and talent for needle-felting adorable tiny rats. There is even now chalk art pointing the way to the shack attached to the railing of her steps at the corner of William and Ostend streets.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: As Gallup officials respond to recent flooding, they say an AI news outlet is getting in the way
item.description: Source NM: “Local officials said in addition to grappling with natural disasters, they were also responding to a new AI news outlet named Prism McKinley County that they say has regularly published false and misleading information in a time of crisis. For instance, within the last week, Prism published a story about a woman drowning in floods, but the death occurred last year, according to Matt Robinson, Gallup’s tourism and marketing manager.”

item.title: Misleading AI-generated doctors pose ‘huge danger to public safety’
item.description: The Guardian: “Misleading health claims online pose a ‘huge danger to public safety’, experts have warned, after research has shown that AI-generated doctors are gaining millions of views on TikTok by spreading dubious health advice.”

item.title: China’s new challenge as natural disasters strike – fake AI videos
item.description: BBC: “Powerful storms and flooding incidents over the last few months have seen fake videos inundating social media platforms – these include images of dead bodies floating in floodwaters, the false depiction of severe flooding in areas actually not affected and others with blatantly fake details of emergency response efforts. In some areas, videos containing false information about power outages prompted residents to panic buy emergency supplies.”

item.title: NV Energy sues to block private arbitration for 2-gigawatt data center projects
item.description: This is Reno: “NV Energy filed a lawsuit Friday in Washoe County Second Judicial District Court seeking to block a private arbitration involving a large proposed data center development. The public utility argues that decisions about electric service, utility planning and customer costs belong exclusively before state utility regulators rather than a private arbitrator.”

item.title: Is Hawthorne Race Course being torn down for a data center? Cicero thinks so.
item.description: Chicago Sun-Times: “Cicero officials believe there could be plans in the works for a data center to replace the Hawthorne Race Course, which recently closed after 135 years of horse racing. In a symbol of how unpopular data center developments have become, the trustees of the near western suburb are expected to consider two resolutions opposing data centers when they meet Tuesday — even though no official announcements have been made about any projects.”

item.title: Professor’s invisible prompt trap catches 32 students cheating on their midterm with AI
item.description: TechSpot: “Modern problems require modern solutions – according to the meme. In this case, the issue is students using AI to cheat on assignments. The solution, used to great effect by one professor, was to hide a white-colored font in the assignment prompt telling the AI to talk nonsense about an unrelated subject.”

item.title: Texas’ multibillion-dollar sales tax exemption for data centers is growing, while audits lag
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Texas’ multibillion-dollar estimate for what it will lose on sales tax breaks for data centers is growing, but the Comptroller’s Office warned lawmakers on Monday they have little information about whether data centers are meeting their promises to be eligible for the exemption.”

item.title: Gov. Kemp backs Georgia data centers despite worries about AI’s risks
item.description: The Current Georgia: “Gov. Brian Kemp weighed in on the rush to develop artificial intelligence, calling the technology ‘scary’ while also welcoming data centers to Georgia and criticizing others who would pause their development.”

item.title: A.I. Companies Are Recruiting Electricians and Carpenters by the Thousands
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “There is no parallel in American history for the boom underway in the construction of data centers, fueled by companies with functionally unlimited cash that are racing to supply skyrocketing demand for their A.I. models. The explosion has offset flagging activity in other sectors, like office construction, which never recovered after the pandemic. Housing has been depressed by high interest rates, and offshore wind felled by political opposition. Still, competition for labor — never mind land and materials — is starting to weigh on other parts of the industry.”

item.title: PwC published reports on AI marred by AI hallucinations
item.description: Financial Times: “PwC published reports on AI and electric vehicles riddled with fake footnotes, misattributed claims and unverifiable information, the latest example of a Big Four firm’s slapdash use of AI-generated content. The AI hallucinations were contained in ‘thought leadership’ reports designed to drum up consulting work for partners in the Middle East, according to an investigation by researchers at GPTZero verified by the FT.”

item.title: Firefox’s New Tab page is getting a daily crossword built from AI-summarized news
item.description: TechSpot: “Mozilla is adding new widgets to Firefox’s New Tab page, including an AI-powered crossword puzzle tied to current news. The feature is powered by Particle, an AI news reader that summarizes articles and uses that material to build a daily puzzle based on the day’s headlines.”

item.title: Indexed Claude Chats Show Why Disallow Is Not Noindex
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Anthropic told TechCrunch that share links will appear in search results only if people post them in accessible locations for crawlers, and that links sent through private messages won’t be indexed…. Google spokesperson Ned Adriance stated that search engines do not determine which pages are made public, and that Google provides site owners with control over crawling and indexing and follows those controls.” You’d think a company awash with so much money would make more effort to protect user privacy.

item.title: Nvidia forms industry alliance for open AI security after Hugging Face hack
item.description: Reuters: “Nvidia said on Monday it had formed a coalition with other companies to develop and share tools for AI safety ​and cybersecurity, days after the Hugging Face incident drew attention to ‌the dangers of losing control of autonomous AI agents.”

item.title: AI chatbots citing Russian propaganda sourced from EU-sanctioned outlet
item.description: Euronews: “AI chatbots are citing Russia propaganda from EU-sanctioned outlets, researchers say, raising questions about how hybrid warfare is expanding to influence large language models (LLMs). Mainstream large language models (LLMs) such as Google Gemini have reportedly cited pro-Russian propaganda from an EU-sanctioned outlet when generating responses, including claims that Ukraine is using the bodies of dead soldiers in meat products.”

item.title: Working to Combat Propaganda in Overlooked Languages
item.description: Dartmouth College: “Anew study led by Fabrice Niyigaba ’27 reports the first digital tool for identifying online propaganda in Kinyarwanda, the national language of Rwanda’s 15 million people—and possibly the first for any of the Bantu languages spoken by 350 million Africans.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Corporate Owners Quietly Reshape Veterinary Care Across CA: Is Your Vet One Of Them?
item.description: Patch California: “That reality is the focus of Private Equity Vet, an independent website that tracks ownership of veterinary hospitals across the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. California dog owner Francis Wong created the database after he says his dachshund, Pluto, died following treatment at a clinic he later discovered was owned by a private equity-backed company.”

item.title: Google’s AI search is rapidly becoming the default, new data shows
item.description: TechCrunch: “AI search is rapidly becoming the default, whether users like it or not. In just a year’s time, Google’s AI-generated answers in search, known as AI Overviews, have gone from appearing in 15% of searches to 43%, according to a new report, driving a shift in how web users consume information online.”

item.title: EBay, former execs to pay $56 million in blogger harassment and stalking case
item.description: CNBC: “Communications revealed in a 2024 criminal complaint brought by federal prosecutors showed senior eBay executives exchanging messages about Ina Steiner, including one where former CEO Devin Wenig said to ‘take her down.’ The couple received a stream of online threats and strange deliveries to their home, including live insects, a funeral wreath, a bloody pig mask and a book about surviving the loss of a spouse.”

item.title: 7 ways to photograph the 2026 total solar eclipse — from smartphone to telescope
item.description: LiveScience: “Photographing a solar eclipse is unlike photographing anything else. Solar safety matters, exposure changes dramatically, and totality lasts only a few precious minutes. Despite that, memorable eclipse photographs can be taken with almost any camera. The best approach depends on your equipment, your experience and what kind of memory you want to bring home.”

item.title: The Creator Economy Has a New Middle Class
item.description: Bloomberg: Mikayla Nogueira is middle class? “In many cases, the followers necessary to sustain a living are smaller (and more attainable) than people might assume. A small but loyal audience can now generate enough income to rival a midlevel salary. Welcome to the middle-class creator economy.”

item.title: Pope’s official prayer app commits cardinal sin, leaks 700K+ users’ info
item.description: The Register: “Click To Pray, a prayer app endorsed by the Pope with hundreds of thousands of users worldwide, has leaked people’s names and email addresses for months – or longer – according to an ethical hacker who said she found and reported the security vulnerability six months ago to no avail. This app needs to take a vow of silence when it comes to your personal information.”

item.title: Wildberries hides military goods in search results after Ukrainian strikes hammer warehouses
item.description: Kyiv Independent: “Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, has stopped displaying military-related goods in response to searches that refer directly to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, according to reports published on July 26. The development comes after seven of the company’s warehouses were hit in a series of Ukrainian strikes beginning July 18. Kyiv has said that the facilities were targeted in order to disrupt Russian army logistics.”

item.title: Ariana Grande sues hackers who leaked music and videos
item.description: BBC: “Pop star Ariana Grande has filed a lawsuit against two unidentified hackers who, she claims, leaked unreleased music and studio footage after gaining access to her collaborators’ computers.”

item.title: Analyzing Toxic Behavior and Its Impact on the Mastodon Community
item.description: ArXiv: “Mastodon as a decentralized federation of independently moderated social servers poses unique challenges for the detection and mitigation of toxic content. There are no unified moderation standards. The ecosystem is very diverse and uneven. This paper explores the development and spread of toxicity in Mastodon, utilizing machine learning methods to examine user posts.”

item.title: Study Shows Extent of Damage to Historic Sites in Syria
item.description: Dartmouth College: “A new Dartmouth study finds that many of Syria’s archaeological sites were damaged not just by looting but that, in areas occupied by the Turkish military, sites were systematically bulldozed…. Using satellite imagery from Google Earth and the European Space Agency’s Pleiades program, researchers analyzed looting and damage at 200 sites throughout Syria.”

item.title: Fark NotNewsletter: Not Ready to go on the cart
item.description: Fark: “Initially I couldn’t believe Google could be so dumb to kill the thing it makes literally all its money from, but lately I’ve arrived at another conclusion: Google knows it’s killing the open web and is doing it on purpose. There’s no way no one at Google realizes what’s happening. There’s no way this hasn’t been brought up internally in meetings. Anyone can see what the impact will be long term. What Google thinks they’ll have for a core business if they succeed in capturing all outbound traffic for themselves, I have no idea. They probably think they’ll be an AI company doing AI stuff making AI revenue, but in my opinion that’s a goal with no clear path, not a plan.”

item.title: Christmas in July: UConn Engineers Capture Gigapixel 3D Video of Snowflakes
item.description: University of Connecticut: “For the first time ever, researchers can witness nanometer-scale thickness changes across a melting snowflake, with a compact, lensless chip that captures gigapixel video at 30 frames per second across centimeter-scale fields.” Good morning, Internet…
